messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Vignette:
Miguel Alvarez had spent most of his adult life on the water, and at 42 he was known among his crew as calm, methodical, and hard to rattle. He was married, lived with his wife in a small house near the port, and worked as a ship captain, a role that had once felt like the clearest expression of who he was. That changed after a man-made disaster at sea, when an ordinary night turn turned into a scene he still struggled to put into words. In his account, the violence of it began with a sudden explosion and then a chain of chaos he could never fully organize in his mind. Objects were hurled during the confusion, and he remembers the sharp, frightening movement of things flying through the air while people shouted over the noise. Later, even now, the sound of a bang can send him back into that moment so quickly that he feels his body tense before he has time to think.

In the aftermath, Miguel found that he was no longer able to move through the world with the same ease. He became preoccupied with whether people around him might be dangerous, scanning faces and bodies for signs that someone could turn aggressive. Military or police uniforms were especially difficult for him to see. Even a glimpse of an officer near the harbor could make him feel as if the air had changed, as though some part of the past were pressing back into the present. He would shift his eyes away, shorten conversations, and focus on getting himself out of the area before the feeling became too strong. He described a growing conviction that he could not rely on other people, not in any deep way. What had happened, in his mind, proved that when things turned dangerous, other people could not be depended on to protect him or make things right.

That belief showed up in the way he organized his days. Miguel began giving up important responsibilities if doing so would keep him away from situations that felt risky or unpredictable. At work, he gradually started letting others take on tasks that had once been his to direct, even when he knew his absence made his own role smaller and less respected. He stopped volunteering for unfamiliar routes and tried to remain with what he knew well, because he avoided unfamiliar places where he could not assess the danger. On land, he became selective about where he sat in restaurants, waiting until he could choose a seat that felt protected, ideally with his back to a wall and an easy view of the room. It was not casual fussiness to him; he experienced it as a practical way to reduce the chance of being caught off guard. Still, the pattern narrowed his life. His wife noticed that he no longer wanted to go to new places with her, and outings that once would have felt simple now required advance planning, scanning, and reassurance.

Sleep became difficult as well. Miguel would lie down at night and find that his mind refused to let go of vigilance. He had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, as if the only safe choice was to keep one part of himself on watch. He remained keyed up by sounds in the neighborhood and by any loud impact that resembled the explosion he remembered. Even in the quiet of his bedroom, he said, he could feel his body listening for danger. The loss of rest made his days feel narrower and more strained, though he did not describe it as exhaustion so much as being unable to fully stand down.

To keep himself occupied and, in his words, to feel something other than dread, Miguel began gambling. He used it as a distraction and to create a quick sense of excitement, especially when he felt himself becoming too alert or too stuck in thought. The brief rush gave him a way to step outside the heaviness, though afterward he often felt unsettled and annoyed with himself. It became part of the small private routines he used to get through evenings when he did not want to think too much. He also worked hard to avoid thinking about the event itself. He was convinced that if he let himself dwell on it, he would not be able to handle what came up. So when the memories surfaced, he pushed them away, changed the subject, or buried himself in something else before they could take shape. He had come to see the people responsible as having faced no consequences, and that sense of unfinished wrongness sat with him in a way he found difficult to resolve.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had been wearing on both his marriage and his work. He was still functioning, but in a more restricted, guarded way, and the strain of keeping himself safe had become harder to manage. What finally brought him in was the realization that he no longer felt like himself at home or on deck, and that his world had gradually shrunk around avoidance, watchfulness, and the need to stay one step ahead of danger. He said he wanted to sleep without feeling he had to remain on guard, and he wanted to believe, if only a little, that his life could be more than waiting for the next bang, the next uniform, or the next sign that something might be thrown.
